result.abstractText: Pneumatic actuation plays a central role in soft robotics, with conventional systems relying on pressure-driven chamber deformation and closed-loop feedback for precise control. Here, we introduce bioinspired ventral-groove filamentary fibers that reframe pneumatic actuation from pressure-dominated chambers to volume-programmable fiber architectures, enabling previously unexplored robotic capabilities. Coupling microgroove unfolding with elastic expansion, these molecularly programmed fibers achieve reversible 400× area expansion at ultralow pressure (∼0.8 kPa) and scale from ∼100 μm to centimeter-scale diameters and tens of meters in length, supporting micro- to macro-scale robotic systems. We demonstrate responsive textile actuation through an everyday flotation garment with 20-m fibers seamlessly integrated into clothing. We also show a gripping approach with three capabilities: disturbance-robust high-precision grasping, conformal handling of fragile nerve-like filaments and delicate incense-ash cones, and open-loop operation that reduces reliance on sensory feedback. By establishing a volume-programmable actuation paradigm, this work paves the way for low-pressure pneumatic technologies in soft robotics and responsive textiles.

result.abstractText: The increasing generation of mixed textile waste and the persistence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and synthetic dyes in industrial effluents present significant challenges for sustainable wastewater treatment. In this study, cotton-acrylic textile waste was valorized into multifunctional magnetic nanofiber adsorbents (CA-Fe₃O₄-NF) via a combined sol-gel-assisted in situ co-precipitation and electrospinning approach. The resulting nanofibers exhibited a hierarchically porous structure, a surface area of 112 m<sup>2</sup> g⁻<sup>1</sup>, and superparamagnetic properties enabling rapid magnetic separation. The developed material demonstrated effective adsorption performance toward PFOS, PFOA, methylene blue, and rhodamine B, with maximum adsorption capacities of 184, 165, 142, and 118 mg g⁻<sup>1</sup>, respectively, along with relatively fast kinetics and spontaneous, endothermic adsorption behavior. The nanofibers retained more than 90% of their initial performance after multiple regeneration cycles, indicating good reusability. Unlike many previously reported magnetic nanofiber adsorbents that rely on virgin polymers and are evaluated under simplified conditions, this study employs waste-derived materials and includes assessment under varying pH, ionic strength, and real wastewater matrices, providing improved environmental relevance. Although the material exhibited potential for simultaneous removal of PFAS and dyes in simplified systems, the study primarily focuses on controlled experimental conditions, and further validation under more complex multi-component environments is required. In addition, the proposed adsorption mechanisms are based on indirect evidence derived from spectroscopic analysis and adsorption behavior, and should therefore be considered as plausible interpretations rather than definitive conclusions. Overall, this work presents a sustainable and cost-effective approach for converting textile waste into functional magnetic nanofiber adsorbents, highlighting their potential application in wastewater treatment while acknowledging the need for further validation under realistic conditions.

result.abstractText: Electronic textiles (e-textiles) are advancing wearable healthcare by integrating electronics into soft, breathable, and scalable fabrics. Composites of cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) and two-dimensional MXenes have gained attention due to their complementary properties. CNFs offer flexibility, mechanical strength, biodegradability, and rich surface chemistry, while MXenes provide high conductivity and tunable multifunctionality. Strong interfacial interactions enable the development of durable, flexible, and environmentally compatible textronic architectures for wearable applications. This review examines the structural role of CNFs in MXene-based textronics across hierarchical formats, from fibers to fabrics. Key fabrication strategies, coating, spinning, electrospinning, and hybrid assembly, are discussed, with emphasis on comfort and performance balance. CNF-MXene textiles enable a range of functions, including wearable energy storage (supercapacitors), physiological and strain/pressure sensing, electrical stimulation, thermotherapy, and controlled drug delivery, positioning them as multifunctional platforms for both power-supporting and therapeutic wearable technologies. Key challenges, such as durability, washability, moisture resistance, and stability, are assessed, with future directions focusing on MXene stability, scalable production, and sustainable end-of-life strategies.
